description:
Hondarribia Castle was built in the 10th century by King Sancho Abarca of Navarre, with a later expansion attributed to Sancho the Strong (1194-1234). When Gipuzkoa passed to Castilian rule in 1200, this strategic fortress became one of the key castles of the Castilian crown, especially favored by the Catholic Monarchs. Emperor Charles V later reformed the building, giving it the name by which it is known today — Castillo de Carlos V.

The building functioned simultaneously as castle and palace, joined by an internal courtyard. In 1966 it passed to the Spanish state, restored and converted into a Parador Nacional, a function it retains today.

Today its rooms sit within the historic building; some overlook the Bay of Txingudi and France beyond, including the property's own "mirador room."

The castle's continuous strategic role from Navarrese fortress to favored Castilian royal stronghold to Habsburg-reformed palace gives Hondarribia a documented history spanning nearly six centuries under three successive political powers.

The building's dual castle-and-palace design, joined internally by a courtyard, reflects the fortress's evolution from a purely military structure into a residence suitable for royal visits.

The castle's position in the Plaza de Armas of Hondarribia's walled old town gives guests staying here a genuinely central base for exploring the town on foot.

faqs.question: Why is Hondarribia Castle also called Castillo de Carlos V?
faqs.answer: Emperor Charles V reformed the building after it became a Castilian royal fortress, giving it the name by which it is still known today.

faqs.question: How central is the castle within Hondarribia?
faqs.answer: Very — it stands in the Plaza de Armas, at the heart of Hondarribia's walled historic old town, making the town easily explorable on foot without a car.

faqs.question: What views does the castle offer?
faqs.answer: Some rooms, including the property's "mirador room," overlook the Bay of Txingudi and France beyond.
